verses.text: Yo, look how lonely the city sits—used to be packed, now ghosted. She was queen of nations, now she’s a servant.
She cries all night, tears nonstop. No one’s there to comfort her. Her old friends ghosted her—turned enemies.
Judah got exiled, crushed by stress, living in foreign lands. No rest, no peace. Her enemies got her boxed in.
Zion’s roads are mourning—no one’s pulling up for the feasts. Her gates are empty, priests sighing, girls grieving. She’s bitter.
Her enemies run the block now. Her haters flex hard. The Lord let it happen—she messed up big time. Her kids got snatched, marched off.
Zion’s beauty faded. Her leaders like deer with no strength—ran till they dropped.
In her darkest hour, Jerusalem remembers the good old days. But now, fallen, mocked by enemies who laugh at her crash.
She sinned heavy—now she’s filthy. Everyone who respected her now disses her. She groans, turns away in shame.
Her mess is out in the open—she didn’t think it’d catch up. Now she’s fallen hard, no one to lift her. “Lord, see my pain,” she cries, “the enemy’s flexing.”
The enemy grabbed all her treasures, even stormed the temple—places they weren’t even allowed.
Her people groan, hunting for food, trading treasures just to survive. “Lord, look—I’m worthless now.”
“Y’all passing by—don’t act like this ain’t major. Ever seen pain like this? The Lord lit me up in His anger.”
“He sent fire to my bones, set traps for my feet, flipped my world. Left me wrecked, weak all day.”
“My sins tied me up like chains—His hand pressed me down. I couldn’t shake it.”
“He crushed my best warriors, called in the squad to wreck me. Crushed my crew like grapes in a winepress.”
“That’s why I cry. My eyes stay leaking. No one’s here to comfort me. My kids are gone—enemy won.”
Zion stretches out her hands—no one helps. The Lord let her enemies surround her. Jerusalem’s now a dirty word.
“The Lord’s right—I rebelled. Listen, all you people, see my pain. My youth got snatched, my fam betrayed me.”
“I called my allies—they ghosted. Priests and elders died in the city, starving, searching for food.”
“Lord, I’m hurting deep. My heart’s wrecked. I’ve been rebellious. Outside, swords take lives; inside, it’s death vibes.”
“They heard me groan, but no one cared. Enemies heard and cheered. You brought this day—let it hit them too.”
“See all my sins, Lord. Judge them like You judged me. I’m crushed, I’m constantly crying.”
How the Lord blacked out Daughter Zion in His anger—threw Israel’s glory from the sky, forgot His footstool like it was nothing.
The Lord wrecked every home in Jacob, no mercy. Tore down Judah’s strongholds, crushed the kingdom and its leaders.
He cut off Israel’s strength like a snapped sword. When enemies came, He dipped His hand back—He burned like fire, eating everything.
He pulled back His bow like an enemy, stood like an opponent. He killed all who looked strong—poured out His fury like fire on Zion.
The Lord became the enemy—He swallowed Israel whole. Tore down palaces, wrecked strongholds, multiplied mourning and moaning.
He trashed His own temple like it was a shack. Ended festivals and Sabbaths. In His fury, He rejected king and priest.
The Lord ditched His altar, disowned His sanctuary. Gave palace walls to the enemy—they shouted in God’s house like it was a party.
The Lord planned to destroy Jerusalem’s wall. He stretched the measuring line, didn’t hold back. He made ramparts and walls mourn—they’re falling together.
Her gates sunk into the ground. He smashed the bars. Her king and leaders are exiled, law’s gone, prophets get no vision.
Elders of Zion sit silent, heads down, dust on them. Girls of Jerusalem hang their heads low.
My eyes are drained from crying, guts twisted. My heart breaks for my people—kids faint in the streets.
They cry to their moms, “Where’s food?” as they collapse in the streets like wounded soldiers, dying in their mothers’ arms.
What can I say to comfort you, Daughter Jerusalem? You’re shattered beyond repair. Who can heal you?
Your prophets gave fake visions—no truth, no callout of sin. Just hype and lies.
Everyone passing by claps and laughs: “Is this the city called perfect beauty, the joy of the earth?”
Your enemies open wide: “We got her! This is the day we waited for!”
The Lord did what He said—He wrecked without mercy. He made enemies rejoice, raised their power.
Cry out to the Lord, wall of Zion. Let your tears flow like a river, day and night. Don’t stop.
Get up, cry out in the night. Pour your heart out like water before the Lord. Lift your hands for your kids—starving on every street.
“Look, Lord! Who’ve You ever treated like this? Should moms eat their own babies? Should priests and prophets be killed in Your sanctuary?”
Young and old lie dead in the streets. You killed them in anger, no mercy.
You called a day of terror—no one escaped. Those I raised and loved, You wiped out.
I’m the one who’s felt the heat—God’s wrath hit me like a freight train.
He dragged me into darkness, no light in sight.
Every move He makes feels like it’s against me.
He broke my bones, wore me down.
Surrounded me with bitterness and pain like a fortress.
He buried me in dark places like I was already dead.
He locked me in, chained me up—I can’t escape.
I cry out, I shout, but He blocks my prayers.
He built stone walls in my path, twisted my steps.
He’s like a lion waiting to pounce, a bear ready to maul.
He ambushed me, tore me up, left me wrecked.
He drew His bow, made me the target.
Arrows straight to the gut—bullseye.
I became the punchline, the joke of the streets.
He filled me with bitterness, made me chug wormwood.
He crushed my teeth with gravel, shoved me in the dirt.
Peace? Gone. I forgot what happiness feels like.
I said, “It’s over. Hope’s dead. God’s done with me.”
I remember the pain, the bitterness—it haunts me.
My soul keeps replaying it, and I’m crushed.
But this I call to mind—and it keeps me going:
God’s mercy never runs out. His love never quits.
It’s fresh every morning. Great is Your faithfulness.
I say, “The Lord is my portion”—so I’ll wait on Him.
The Lord’s good to those who wait, to the soul that seeks Him.
It’s good to hope quietly, to wait for God to show up.
It’s good to carry the yoke young—learn the weight early.
Sit alone, stay silent—God’s the One who laid it on you.
Put your face in the dirt—maybe there’s still hope.
Let them slap your cheek, take the hits—don’t fight back.
The Lord won’t reject forever.
Even if He lets you suffer, He’ll show compassion—His love runs deep.
He doesn’t enjoy hurting people or crushing them.
When people get stomped in prison,
when justice gets twisted in court,
when someone’s rights get denied—doesn’t the Lord see it all?
Who can speak and make it happen unless the Lord says so?
Don’t both good and bad come from the mouth of the Most High?
Why should anyone complain when punished for their sins?
Let’s check ourselves, audit our ways, and turn back to God.
Let’s lift our hearts and hands to heaven:
“We’ve sinned, rebelled—You haven’t forgiven.”
You wrapped Yourself in anger, hunted us down, showed no mercy.
You covered Yourself with a cloud—our prayers couldn’t break through.
You made us trash, rejected by the nations.
Everyone’s clowning us, mouths wide open.
Fear and traps all around—ruin and wreckage.
My eyes flood with tears for my people’s destruction.
My tears won’t stop till the Lord looks down and sees.
I’m crying nonstop till He notices.
My heart breaks for the daughters of my city.
My enemies hunted me like a bird, for no reason.
They threw me in a pit, dropped stones on me.
Water rose over my head—I said, “It’s a wrap.”
I called Your name, Lord, from the pit’s bottom.
You heard me beg—“Don’t ignore my cry.”
You came close when I called: “Don’t be scared.”
You took my case, Lord. You saved my life.
You saw the wrong done to me—bring justice.
You saw their hate, all their plots.
You heard their trash talk, their schemes.
The whispers, the shade they throw all day.
Look at them mocking me nonstop.
Pay them back, Lord, for what they’ve done.
Blind them with Your judgment.
Chase them down in anger—wipe them out from under heaven.
How the gold lost its shine! Even the purest drip looks dusty. Sacred stones scattered on every street.
Zion’s precious kids—once worth their weight in gold—now treated like cheap clay pots.
Even jackals nurse their young, but my people? Cold. Daughters of Zion act cruel like desert ostriches.
Babies’ tongues stick to the roof of their mouths from thirst. Kids beg for bread—no one breaks them off a piece.
Those who used to eat fancy now starve in the streets. Once dripped in purple, now hugging trash piles.
Daughter of my people punished worse than Sodom—wiped out in a flash, no warning.
Her princes were cleaner than snow, whiter than milk, glowing like jewels.
Now their faces are darker than soot, unrecognizable in the streets. Skin shriveled tight on bones—dried out like wood.
Better to die by sword than starve—slow death hits harder.
Compassionate women cooked their own kids—ate their babies during the collapse.
The Lord’s fury hit max level. He poured out His anger, lit up Zion like a wildfire.
No one believed it—kings, nations—nobody thought Jerusalem would fall like this.
But it happened cuz of her prophets’ sins, her priests’ guilt—shedding innocent blood in the city.
They wandered blind in the streets, defiled with blood, no one dared touch their clothes.
People shouted: “Unclean! Move away!” They ran, scattered, but even the nations said, “Don’t stay here.”
The Lord Himself scattered them. He won’t look their way. Priests get no respect, elders no honor.
We watched and waited for help that never came. We kept looking to nations that couldn’t save.
They hunted our steps—we couldn’t walk the streets. Our end was near, days numbered, game over.
Our pursuers were faster than eagles. They chased us through mountains, ambushed us in the wilderness.
Our very breath—the Lord’s anointed—was caught in their traps. We thought, “He’ll protect us among the nations.”
Rejoice while you can, Edom. Party in Uz. But your turn’s coming—the cup will hit your lips too.
Zion’s punishment is done—He won’t exile you again. But Edom? He’ll expose your sins, and you’ll catch yours next.
Lord, remember what went down. Look at our pain. Don’t ghost us.
Our land’s been snatched, homes handed to strangers.
We’re orphans now—no dads. Our moms barely hanging on.
We pay to drink our own water. Even firewood costs us.
We’re hunted nonstop—no rest, no breathers.
We begged Egypt and Assyria for food—just to stay alive.
Our ancestors sinned and dipped. We’re the ones paying the price.
Slaves rule over us now. No one steps in to save.
We risk our lives just to eat—swords in the wild could drop us.
Our skin’s burnt like an oven—fever from hunger.
Women violated in Zion, girls abused in Judah’s streets.
Princes hanged by enemies, elders disrespected.
Young men forced to grind grain, boys collapsed under wood loads.
Elders vanished from the gates, young men stopped their music.
Joy’s gone. Dancing’s dead. Our hearts are heavy, our heads hang low.
The crown’s fallen. We messed up—this is on us.
Our hearts are wrecked, eyes dim with tears.
Mount Zion’s a wasteland—foxes roam what used to be holy.
But You, Lord, rule forever. Your throne’s eternal.
Why You still ghosting us? How long You gonna stay silent?
Bring us back to You, Lord—we’ll come running. Make us new again, like the old days.
Unless You’ve totally rejected us… unless You’re done with us for good.
